newsitem.title: UK: SOCCER-SHOWCASE-JUNINHO AND EMERSON HOPING FOR FINAL SAMBA.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER-SHOWCASE-JUNINHO AND EMERSON HOPING FOR FINAL SAMBA.

text.p: Given the choice of all the great stadiums in all the great clubs around the world, Brazilian international Juninho walked into Middlesbrough's.
Even more surprisingly, compatriots Branco, albeit briefly, and Emerson followed him.
Not that there is anything remotely amiss about the two-year-old glass and steel Riverside Stadium which epitomises the wholesale facelift undergone by many of England's top clubs.

It is just that the Middlesbrough side that play there was, and still is, one of the most unsuccessful big clubs in England without a major trophy to its name in 121 years of almost continual under-achieving.
The club's location in the heartland of the industrial north east, dominated by chemical works and factory chimneys, does not win it many awards for scenic beauty.

But the boys from Brazil did not come to the area -- known as England's "soccer hotbed" -- for the view. They came because in the harsh world of soccer business in the 1990s every player has his price and if the package is right, his boots are on the dressing room peg as soon as the ink is dry on the contract.
The Middlesbrough fans took to Juninho, now 24, immediately and he is revered in the area where he lives with his family in a village away from the city.

Emerson, 25, has endeared himself too, turning up for 70s disco nights in the clubs wearing flares without a trace of embarrassment. Well, if you do look like a missing member of Kool and The Gang no one is going to argue with you.
And 18 months since Juninho's highly publicised arrival from Sao Paulo is the autumn of 1985, much has changed at Middlesbrough.

The club have just been relegated to the first division, they have appeared in the first major final in their history, losing to Leicester City in the replayed League Cup Final last month, and on Saturday make their first ever appearance in the F.A. Cup Final.

And as if to underline the club's schizophrenic form, Juninho and Emerson have largely dazzled but occasionally disappointed throughout the campaign and they both return to Wembley with something to prove in what could well be the last game they play for the club.

Juninho, whose performances became more and more inspired the tougher Middlesbrough's fight against relegation became, returns to Wembley six weeks after being man-marked out of the League Cup Final by Pontuus Kamaark of Leicester.

Emerson, who appears to have settled down after his unauthorised trips back home earlier in the season landed him with huge club fines, could grace English soccer's showpiece with one of his dazzling goals. Or he could give one of those displays when he disappears into blind alleys.

Juninho, has just been voted runner-up to Chelsea's Gianfranco Zola as England's Footballer of the Year, and in full flight, with the ball at his feet, running at defences, there are few more exciting sights in the game.
Despite his diminutive size, he has great strength and seemingly endless energy which help him cover every centimetre of the pitch.
Atletico Madrid and Valencia are rumoured to have made bids of 8.0 million pounds sterling ($13 million) nearly double the amount Middlesbrough paid for him.
Emerson's future is also in some doubt, and he could be heading back to Portugal where he last played with Porto, or possibly moving to Spain.
With relegation now a certainty not even winning the F.A. Cup will guarantee they stay at Middlesbrough.
Juninho's arrival at Middlesbrough was seen at the time to be the start of a new era for the club, and it certainly was that. Defeat to Chelsea on Saturday will bring that era to a close.
Saturday could well provide the final Samba party for Middlesbrough. If it does, for the fans, it will all be over far too fast.
